description: A group composed of Software Engineering students from UFG and Artificial Intelligence researchers from CEIA (Center of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence). We combine technical rigor in the development of scalable systems with practical experience in the research and implementation of AI models, focused on transforming complex problems into functional, high-impact solutions.
summary: Apollo 62 is an offline, browser-based decision-support prototype that helps astronauts assess their own health. It compares heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep and mood with each astronaut's pre-flight baseline, and shows the result on a body map using colour, icon and text. A single mode switch adapts the whole platform to Earth, Space Station, Moon or Spacecraft, changing communication delay, escalation, radiation dose, exercise and routine. Orbit, the onboard chat assistant, was designed and built by our team. Its answers come from our own rule engine and a curated library of passages, and it runs locally without any external service. Orbit explains the data and suggests safe next steps, but status and alerts always come from our deterministic rules. Every number is labelled REAL or SIMULATED with its source. The prototype addresses the challenge's call for a visual self-assessment tool with guidance across mission environments. It covers the five NASA HRP hazards and the requested indicators, replays a real NASA DONKI solar event that triggers a shelter flow, and drafts compact reports for the ground. This matters because on deep-space missions a reply from Earth can take up to 24 minutes and blackouts can last weeks. Crews need Earth-independent support to spot changes early and know when to escalate, with humans kept in the loop.
details:
Under the hood, every screen reads from a single store and from a set of pure TypeScript rules, so the same inputs always produce the same status. The rules turn deviations into levels and environment delays into reply estimates. They also turn the solar event into postponed exercise, and the crew's factors into a hazard outlook. A slow drift over several days raises an early warning even while a value is still within range. Crew members log readings and check-ins, and those inputs update the charts and the outlook immediately. When the astronaut decides to escalate, the copilot assembles a package of facts and actions already taken, which the astronaut reviews before it is queued for Earth.

For the crew, the benefit is confidence in the long gap before help arrives. They have a clear picture of their own trends, the next safe step and the right moment to call the medical officer. For flight surgeons, it means short, structured updates instead of raw data streams. We intend the prototype to show that Earth-independent self-assessment can be safe, transparent and light enough to run on any laptop. The same design could later take data from wearables and biosensors, and could serve remote settings on Earth such as polar stations, offshore platforms and rural clinics.

We built it with React 19, TypeScript in strict mode and Vite, with Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui on Radix for accessible components. Recharts draws the charts, Zustand holds the state and Zod validates every fixture and input. The rules are covered by Vitest unit tests. The optional language model runs in a Web Worker through WebLLM and WebGPU, with a deterministic protocol engine as the default. Fonts and assets are bundled locally, the app is hosted on Vercel, and it needs only an ordinary laptop and browser.

The idea is creative because it combines things that health dashboards usually keep apart. Communication delay becomes a design input. Each crew member's normal is personal and recalculated after each change of environment. Prevention is built around NASA's own hazard list rather than generic wellness tips. The AI acts as a careful translator of the rules rather than as an oracle.

Our team weighed several factors. On the regulatory side, the prototype makes no diagnosis or treatment claims and always shows a "not a medical device" notice. We kept humans in the loop, and the AI fails safely when it errs. We used synthetic data because real astronaut records are restricted. Each source has its own terms of use, which we checked. Usability under fatigue and stress led us to calm visuals, sentence case and keyboard support. Finally, we limited scope deliberately to a complete, working core flow, leaving sensors, a backend and clinically validated thresholds for future work.
